comments.body:
Is 

> this may be a false positive if your program uses some custom stack unwind mechanism, swapcontext or vfork

relevant? cc @vstinner

I have following repro:
```python
import faulthandler
import sys


faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(10 * 1e-308, exit=True, file=sys.__stderr__)
assert False
```

It fails with assert in the C code:
```
Running Debug|x64 interpreter...
Traceback (most recent call last):
Timeout (0:00:00.000001)!
Thread 0x00006e38 (most recent call first):
  File "X:\Work\cpython\main\Lib\traceback.py"  File "X:\Work\cpython\issues\b140815.py", line 8, in <module>
    assert False
           ^^^^^
Assertion failed: !PyStackRef_IsNull(f->f_executable), file X:\Work\cpython\main\Include\internal\pycore_interpframe.h, line 21
AssertionError
```

If no one minds, I'd like to take a look.

This segfault occurs because the `faulthandler_thread` runs concurrently with interpreter finalization. 

This happens because the `timeout` value of the `dump_traceback_later` is `10 * 1e-308` which is cropped to 1us. Therefore, the `faulthandler_thread` runs as soon as possible. 

`faulthandler_thread` doesn't use any synchronization primitives, so it is not a thread-safe, even in the GIL-enabled build.

I found an issue https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/128400 and a PR https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/128422 where the call to the `StopTheWorld` function was added to the `faulthandler_dump_traceback_py_impl` to prevent multithreading issues in the no-GIL build. Therefore, I believe this approach is valid for this issue as well. For the GIL-enabled build, I added the GIL acquisition.

@sergey-miryanov:
> This segfault occurs because the faulthandler_thread runs concurrently with interpreter finalization.

`_Py_DumpTracebackThreads()` is called by the `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later()` thread while the main thread is freeing its frame.

`_Py_DumpTracebackThreads()` reads freed memory and does crash randomly. It already calls `_PyMem_IsPtrFreed()` in a few places to detect freed memory, but it's not enough.

> faulthandler_thread doesn't use any synchronization primitives, so it is not a thread-safe, even in the GIL-enabled build.

This is by design. `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(exit=True)` dumps the traceback and exits the process to implement a software watchdog. It is used by buildbots and other CIs to exit after a timeout.

`faulthandler.dump_traceback_later()` should not attempt to acquire the GIL or any other lock since it's used to dump the traceback in case in other deadlocks.

I wrote https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/140921 to fix the issue: detect if a frame object or a code object is invalid or freed.

With my fix, I can no longer reproduce the crash: I ran the script in a loop for 1 minute.

> `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later()` should not attempt to acquire the GIL or any other lock since it's used to dump the traceback in case in other deadlocks.

Thanks to point me this! It was not clear to me after reading the documentation (it is only one reference to the `deadlock` on the page and I just missed it).

Dummy example of deadlock:

```py
import faulthandler
import threading

def work():
    lock = threading.Lock()
    lock.acquire()
    lock.acquire()
    lock.release()
    lock.release()

faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(5, exit=True)
work()
faulthandler.cancel_dump_traceback_later()
```

Output:

```
Timeout (0:00:05)!
Thread 0x00007fc30261ebc0 [python] (most recent call first):
  File "/home/vstinner/python/main/x.py", line 7 in work
  File "/home/vstinner/python/main/x.py", line 12 in <module>
```

faulthandler shows where the deadlock occurs.

> faulthandler shows where the deadlock occurs.

I can use this at work somehow 🤔 ... Thanks!

Instead of crashing, the [initial reproducer](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/140815#issue-3574261278) now completes with incomplete traceback like:

```
$ ./python x.py
Timeout (0:00:00.000001)!
Thread 0x00007f107d86bbc0 [python] (most recent call first):
  File "/home/vstinner/python/main/Lib/tokenize.py", line ??? in find_cookie
  <invalid frame>
```

Even if, as I explained in other comments, it's not 100% reliable. I consider that the initial issue has been fixed and I close the issue. Thanks for your bug report.
